facts.text: The opening theme song tells viewers that Herman Farbage, the garbage man from the 1978 original, wasn't killed after all and now has his own TV show.
The theme song jokes about a part three. Sure enough, director John De Bello made two more sequels: Killer Tomatoes Strike Back! (1991) and Killer Tomatoes Eat France! (1992).
Anthony Starke (Chad Finletter) later played Jimmy, the guy who speaks of himself in the third person, in the 1995 Seinfeld episode "The Jimmy."
Karen M. Waldron, who plays Tara Boumdeay, was born Karen Mistal, and some listings still credit her that way. She later acted in Space Cowboys (2000).
A pizzeria patron here is future U.S. congressman Gary Condit, a friend of co-writer J. Stephen Peace from the California Assembly. He became a household name in the 2001 Chandra Levy case.
J. Stephen Peace, who plays pizza-shop owner Wilbur Finletter, co-wrote and produced the film. He later served in the California State Assembly and Senate.
In the first film, the awful song "Puberty Love" was sung by director John De Bello's 14-year-old neighbor Matt Cameron, who grew up to drum for Soundgarden and Pearl Jam.
Before filming, John Astin (Professor Gangreen) asked director John De Bello if he should watch the original Attack of the Killer Tomatoes. De Bello told him not to bother.
Steve Lundquist, who plays Igor, is a real Olympic champion: he won gold in the 100-meter breaststroke and 400-meter medley relay at the 1984 Los Angeles Games.
Look at the wall clocks behind Professor Gangreen: one reads "Las Vegas" and has no hands, likely a nod to casinos famously having no clocks.
George Clooney (Matt Stevens) was an unknown here. His breakthrough came in 1994 as Dr. Doug Ross on ER, earning two Emmy nominations.
Fuzzy Tomato's cuddly-pest look fits the film's long spoof list, which includes the Star Trek episode "The Trouble with Tribbles" (1967) and E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982).
George Clooney reportedly had fun making the film but was glad it didn't do well enough to typecast him, according to a FemaleFirst interview cited by Yahoo Entertainment.
Anthony Starke (Chad Finletter) next turned up in the 1989 James Bond film Licence to Kill, one year after this goofy tomato sequel.
Clips of the original Attack of the Killer Tomatoes aired on the cartoon Muppet Babies, which helped the film's cult following grow before this sequel arrived.
Karen Waldron (Tara Boumdeay) next appeared in the delightfully titled Cannibal Women in the Avocado Jungle of Death (1989), then on Baywatch.
The film was shot in the South Bay area of San Diego County, including National City and Chula Vista.
Charles White, the pushy TV reporter, is played by the film's own director and co-writer John De Bello. He later plays the harried director who yells that the production is out of money.
The poster was first painted as a Campbell's Soup can with John Astin's face on the label. Over copyright worries, artist David R. Darrow's new label was physically glued over it.
The film jokes that it's out of money, but the real budget was reportedly about $1 million. It reportedly grossed around $5 million in the U.S.
Richard Scheib of Moria gave the film one star, yet called the product placement gags its most amusing element, since they serve as the film's answer to its cash shortage.
The product placement joke was also a real one: per Richard Scheib of Moria, Pepsi logos show up on Gangreen's lab coat and the lab exterior, plus a Kellogg's box.
Critics were unkind: Rotten Tomatoes lists 0% from 6 reviews, and TV Guide called the film an "unnecessary sequel." Emanuel Levy gave it 2 out of 5.
The franchise grew from a UC Davis student project and was inspired by the Japanese film Matango, retitled Attack of the Mushroom People on U.S. TV. The 1978 original cost roughly $120,000.
This was among George Clooney's first big-screen roles, after Grizzly II: The Revenge, which sat unreleased for years. He didn't return for the 1991 and 1992 Killer Tomatoes sequels.
Co-writer and production designer Costa Dillon plays several roles, billed as "C.J. Clark Dillon," then "Dillon again, who else," then "Guess who?" The credits also run backward, cast last.
Teri Weigel, who plays Matt's playmate, was a real Playboy Playmate (April 1986) and appeared on the cover of Playboy's November 1985 Women of Mensa issue.
In the Playboy issue George Clooney holds up, there's a Vidal Sassoon ad starring Steve Lundquist, the Olympic swimmer who plays Igor.
Chris Coffel of Bloody Disgusting compared it to The Simpsons: so many jokes you can't catch them in one viewing, a movie made for the VHS generation.
The first film's theme was played on January 13, 1990 as a wake-up call for Space Shuttle Columbia's crew, a joke since Columbia was retrieving 12.5 million tomato seeds.
DVD Talk's Adam Tyner wrote that the film "doesn't just break the fourth wall; it grinds it into a fine powder," with humor years ahead of its time.
John Astin said in a 2023 retrospective documentary that his Professor Gangreen was partly inspired by his father, a real scientist who worked on a death ray for the U.S. government.
During the 1978 original, a rented helicopter crashed and was totaled, a $60,000 loss, though nobody was seriously hurt. Peace also nearly died in a car-chase stunt.
VultureHound's Lee Hazell likened the film to the Marx Brothers' manic energy and the Zucker brothers' gleeful stupidity, but docked a point for turning tomatoes into machine-gun-toting Chippendales.
The prison scenes were shot at a real facility: the Richard J. Donovan Correctional Facility on Alta Road in San Diego, one of the film's listed locations.
Rick Rockwell, who plays Jim Richardson, later became infamous as the groom on the 2000 TV special Who Wants to Marry a Multi-Millionaire?
Dread Central's Anthony Arrigo called it a "zany riot" whose gags fly so fast it's almost impossible to catch every joke the first time, comparing it to Zucker/Abrams and Mel Brooks.
The end credits run in reverse of the industry norm: crew first, musicians before the midpoint, and the main cast last.
The old woman who halts the credits to insist that viewers stay is said to be the director's mother, according to a Yahoo Entertainment retrospective by Stephen Wilds.
The post-credits scene, where carrot soldiers gun down the hosts, ends with Gangreen's laugh and "See you in France!", teasing sequel Killer Tomatoes Eat France! (1992).
